title: This Is All They Want
author: The Daily Dad
summary: This short Daily Dad piece confronts fathers and husbands with a blunt argument: doing the bare minimum at home, assuming your partner will pick up the slack, then expecting praise on the rare occasion you contribute, is not good enough, even if it's 'better than some men.' Citing a lyric from Paris Paloma's 'Stem the Flow,' the author argues that families don't need grand gestures or perfection from the men in their lives; they need consistent, unprompted effort and attention. The piece points to Eve Rodsky's book Fair Play as a concrete tool for making household labor visible and equitably shared rather than defaulted to one partner. Its underlying claim is that a father's stated priorities mean nothing if his family doesn't experience his best effort day to day.
points: Stop treating partial effort as acceptable just because it's better than the worst stereotype of fathers and husbands.
Recognize that a spouse's or child's ask isn't for a grand gesture but for consistent effort and attention.
Use tools like Eve Rodsky's 'Fair Play' system to make invisible household labor visible and divided, rather than waiting to be asked.
Build a daily reflection practice to notice where you're coasting on family responsibilities before your spouse has to point it out.
quotes: It's a stereotype to be sure, and you're not nearly as bad as some men.
Your job is to do your job—to take care of your family, to carry your share of the load and then some.
Your spouse, your kids, want you to try. Is that so hard? To try to care? To try to notice?
They don't need perfection. They don't need some grand gesture. They need effort. They need attention.
They need to know that the family you say matters most to you actually gets the best of you, too.
